LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Dragonfly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fastest card at three speeds: your toddler hovers like a dragonfly, darts once, then freezes mid-air — and lands gently on a lily pad, just the way the real flyer does.

What is this?

A dragonfly is a long, thin insect with four glittering wings that zips over ponds and streams, hovers in one spot, then darts off after smaller bugs. It is one of the best flyers in the whole garden.

What does it mean?

Hover-dart-freeze is a toddler movement masterpiece: three speeds in one body, ending in the dramatic mid-air stop. And the pond setting makes it the perfect card for practising water-safety rules in play form.

What does the child need to know?

Dragonflies zoom and hover near water, and they are look-at friends like everyone in the set. Near any real pond or stream, a grown-up holds the hand — the wings stay in the air game, well away from the water’s edge.

Why this matters

The freeze is the secret prize: stopping mid-action is real impulse control, dressed as a dragonfly trick. Pairing it with the pond rule means the quickest card in the set quietly teaches its calmest lesson.

What it teaches

Speed switching (hover, dart, freeze), balance on soft landings, pond-and-water vocabulary, and the safety habit of hand-holding near water, rehearsed long before it is ever needed.

Words to learn

dragonflywingszoomfreezepondgentle

Say this to your child

“"Zoom! A dragonfly — four shiny wings! Can you hover? Now dart... and freeze, right in the air, like this! Dragonflies fly over ponds, and ponds mean we hold a grown-up’s hand. Soft wings, soft landings, still feet by the water."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say dragonfly — then point out the wings: this flyer wears a shiny set of them.
  2. Be a dragonfly together: arms out wide, hover in one spot, then dart two steps sideways — and freeze! Mid-air, mid-word, everywhere.
  3. Spread cushions as lily pads and fly from pad to pad, touching down softly each time — a dragonfly lands like a feather.
  4. Tell the water story simply: real dragonflies live by ponds, and ponds are grown-up-hand places — we visit with fingers linked.
  5. End with three speeds on request: hover... dart... freeze! Then one last feather landing to finish.

Look closer at the picture

Say dragonfly together and find the shiny wings on the card — this dragonfly has wings that glint. Ask your toddler to flap their own wings once, then make them go still as the card.

Ask your child

"What does the dragonfly do?" "Can you hover and freeze?" "Where do dragonflies fly — over what?" "What do our hands do near a pond?" — answered with a zoom, a freeze and a linked-hand gesture.

What your child can say or do

"Zoom, freeze!" played down corridors at top speed and full stop, dragonflies announced at every puddle and pond, and mid-air freezes held with tremendous seriousness — the stop is the trophy move.

Out in the real world

Dragonflies patrol ponds, canals and damp meadows all summer, often resting on reeds and railings. Each sighting is a rerun: hover-watch quietly, then move on with feet safe and hand held near water.

Try it together

Mid-air statues: dance and dart while a song plays, then freeze like a hovering dragonfly when it stops — wings out, one foot up if brave. The stopping is the game, and the giggles are the reward.

Understanding check

Call freeze during ordinary play tomorrow: an instant statue means the dragonfly left its trick behind — self-control arrived on four glittering wings, exactly as designed.

Parent tips

Practise the freeze before the zoom — stopping on cue is the skill worth polishing. Mention the hand-holding rule cheerfully at bath time too; water rules work best when they are rehearsed everywhere.

Staying safe

Real dragonflies live at the water’s edge, so pond and stream visits happen hand-in-hand with a grown-up and never at a run. Dragonflies themselves are harmless — looked at, never caught, and left to their buzzing.

This lesson pairs with the Dragonfly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).
